title: The Housing Lark
description: A comic novel of West Indian London, published by MacGibbon & Kee in 1965, in which Battersby and his friends try to pool their savings to buy a house. The Lynne Rienner synopsis calls it Selvon's fifth novel; by the dates of the first editions it is his sixth.
plot_or_argument: Faced with unscrupulous and racist landlords, Battersby, a West Indian exile in London, and his rakish friends hatch a scheme to pool their money for a place of their own, but it does not go as planned (Caribbean Beat). The search for decent, affordable shelter brings hardships and comic situations and shows the exiles' dealings with English women, with the British in general and with one another (Lynne Rienner synopsis). The Northern Arizona University essay notes that the lark remains a lark to Battersby but becomes a grim commitment for Jean, and that at a community fete the Indo-Trinidadian Syl, asked why he does not go back to India, answers, 'Brit'n is my country'.
narrative_structure: An ensemble comedy organised around the house-buying scheme.
principal_characters: Battersby ('Bat'), who devises the scheme; Syl, an Indo-Trinidadian; Jean
meter_and_prosody: Caribbean Beat calls it a cheeky comedy of a West Indian exile's search for shelter.
historical_context: Set in London in the early 1960s, when West Indian migrants met discrimination from landlords; published in 1965.
literary_significance: Selvon's second novel of West Indian London; reissued by Lynne Rienner, Boulder, in 1990.
bibliographical_notes: First edition: MacGibbon & Kee, London, 1965 (South Asian Britain). Reissued by Lynne Rienner, Boulder, 1990 (Toronto Metropolitan University Library).
thematic_analysis: Housing and racism in 1960s London, a migrant community forming out of separate struggles (the essay contrasts it with the 'lonely' struggles of the earlier novel), the price of assimilation, and the claim to belong.
summary: A scheme to buy a house together, and the gatherings, outings and quarrels of the West Indians drawn into it.
research_notes: Not read. The account rests on the publisher's synopsis reprinted by Toronto Metropolitan University Library and on search-result extracts from Caribbean Beat and the Northern Arizona University essay; Jean's relation to Battersby is not stated in them.

title: The Plains of Caroni
description: Published by MacGibbon & Kee in London in 1970, the novel grew out of research on Trinidad's sugar industry sponsored by Tate and Lyle, which financed Selvon's return visit in 1969 (Journal of West Indian Literature, citing Michel Fabre). It turns on the trial of a mechanical cane harvester on a sugar estate.
plot_or_argument: Romesh, a university-educated agricultural scientist working for the management of a fictionalised Caroni Ltd., oversees the testing of a new harvesting machine on the estate where his family cuts cane. The labourers fear, rightly, that it will cost them their jobs, and suspect it of being a 'metal Trojan horse'. The old cutter Balgobin, whose love for Seeta was thwarted by her arranged marriage to his brother, has given his life to the craft of cutting, and he resists the harvester with his cutlass. As he is dying, he is saved from arrest by the revelation that Romesh, raised as his nephew, is his son. Romesh leaves for London with his white girlfriend, while Balgobin is venerated as a hero.
narrative_structure: Centred on the harvester trial and its consequences, ending with Balgobin's death and Romesh's departure.
principal_characters: Balgobin, an old cane-cutter; Romesh, an agricultural scientist, raised as his nephew; Teeka, Romesh's brother, a cane-cutter; Seeta, whom Balgobin loved
meter_and_prosody: The journal essay quotes the rhythm of Balgobin's cutting ('his arm arcing the air ... in a grace of movement') and the villagers' images for the harvester: 'magic machine', 'space machine', 'giant monster'.
historical_context: Tate and Lyle was preparing to leave Trinidad: in 1970 it sold a majority share in Caroni Ltd. to the PNM government, and it ended its involvement in 1976. Romesh cites the figures Selvon gathered, 1.94 man-days to produce a ton of sugar in Hawaii against 15.21 in Trinidad.
literary_significance: Selvon turned it into the radio play Harvest in Wilderness (collected in Highway in the Sun, 1991). Its readers include a 1995 study of its idea of heroism, Supriya Agarwal's 'Conflict and Resolution' (2008), the ecocritical issue of the Journal of West Indian Literature (2016) and Kris Singh's essay on cane in Anthurium (2025).
bibliographical_notes: First edition: MacGibbon & Kee, London, 1970 (South Asian Britain; Journal of West Indian Literature). Reissued by Williams-Wallace, Toronto, 1985 (Anthurium's references).
thematic_analysis: Mechanisation and the decline of sugar (the Journal of West Indian Literature essay reads the novel as foreshadowing oil's triumph over sugar in Trinidad), the dignity and skill of manual labour, hidden paternity, and the gulf between an educated, creolised generation and the cane-cutters.
summary: An Indo-Trinidadian cane-cutting family and the trial of a mechanical harvester on a fictionalised Caroni estate, ending with an old cutter's fight against the machine.
research_notes: Not read. The plot rests on two independent scholarly discussions seen as search-result extracts (the Journal of West Indian Literature essay and 'The Novel since 1970'), which agree, except that the second calls Romesh a plantation manager and the first an agricultural scientist working for the management.

title: Those Who Eat the Cascadura
description: Published in London by Davis Poynter in 1972, a novel of interracial love on a Trinidad plantation, framed by an obeahman's prophecy.
plot_or_argument: Manko, the village obeahman, predicts trouble when an Englishman, Garry, comes to stay, and the prophecy is fulfilled when Garry falls in love with a local Indian woman, Sarojini (Caribbean Beat; Northern Arizona University essay). The essay reads the outcome as racism proving stronger than love, since Garry feels she cannot be transplanted from the world that made her, and notes the discovery that Roger Franklin, the plantation owner, secretly visits Indian women at night and is probably Sarojini's father.
narrative_structure: Framed by Manko's prophecy and by its fulfilment in Garry's love affair.
principal_characters: Manko, the village obeahman; Garry, an Englishman; Sarojini, a young Indian woman; Roger Franklin, the plantation owner
meter_and_prosody: Caribbean Beat calls it a story of interracial romance and the chaos it creates in a village; the essay sees the distant thunder of I Hear Thunder grown into a hurricane threatening the whole society.
historical_context: Published in London in 1972, six years before Selvon left Britain; it was reissued in Toronto by TSAR in 1988.
literary_significance: At his death Selvon was negotiating a film adaptation (Dawes).
bibliographical_notes: First edition: Davis Poynter, London, 1972 (South Asian Britain). Reissued by TSAR, Toronto, 1988 (Toronto Metropolitan University Library).
thematic_analysis: Interracial love and the sexual history of the plantation, which the essay calls a practice as old as slavery; obeah and prophecy; and the outsider's romantic idea of the island.
summary: An Englishman's stay on a friend's Trinidad estate, his love for a young Indian woman and the prophecy of the village obeahman.
research_notes: Not read. Garry, Sarojini and Roger Franklin are named only in the Northern Arizona University essay, seen as a search-result extract; the rest of the account comes from a Caribbean Beat extract.

title: Moses Ascending
description: The second novel of the Moses trilogy, published in London by Davis Poynter in 1975, returns to Moses Aloetta of The Lonely Londoners, now the owner of a ramshackle house in Shepherd's Bush who means to write his memoirs while his handyman does the work. Wikipedia names it, with The Lonely Londoners, as the book for which Selvon is best known.
plot_or_argument: Moses, once a poor Caribbean immigrant, has become the proud landlord of a ramshackle house in Shepherd's Bush. He sees himself as master of his own domain, writing his memoirs while his trusty sidekick and handyman, Bob, does all the work. His troubles are far from over. A Black Power group takes over the basement, headed by the indomitable Brenda; an illegal people-smuggling ring is discovered upstairs (an AbeBooks description of the first edition says Moses shelters Pakistani immigrants); and there is harassment by racist police, sheep-slaughtering in the back yard and a Black Panther on the loose. The publisher's description asks whether Moses' 'elaborately constructed castle in the air' will be demolished by these unruly forces, and presents the book as following the fortunes of characters from The Lonely Londoners.
narrative_structure: Set largely in Moses' house, from the basement taken by the Black Power group to the upper floor where the smuggled immigrants are found; the episodes arise from its tenants and visitors.
principal_characters: Moses Aloetta, landlord and would-be memoirist; Bob, his handyman; Brenda, leader of the Black Power group
meter_and_prosody: Dawes counts the three Moses novels as a comic trilogy, and the publisher calls the book a hilarious and telling depiction of 1970s Britain.
historical_context: Its Black Power group, people-smuggling and police harassment place it in the London of the early 1970s. It appeared in 1975, the year Selvon took up his fellowship at Dundee, three years before he left Britain for Canada.
literary_significance: After The Lonely Londoners the best known of Selvon's books (Wikipedia). It continues the Moses saga, which Dawes takes as Selvon's most telling treatment of identity and belonging, and its characters reappear in the radio plays of Eldorado West One (1988). It has been reissued by Heinemann (1984) and Penguin (2008, and in Penguin Modern Classics).
bibliographical_notes: First edition: Davis Poynter, London, 1975 (South Asian Britain; an AbeBooks listing of the first edition spells the publisher 'David-Poynter', ISBN 0706701887). Heinemann, London, 1984 (cited by Wikipedia); Penguin, London, 2008 (Toronto Metropolitan University Library); Penguin Modern Classics, ISBN 9780241504390.
thematic_analysis: The comedy of upward mobility, as the former tenant becomes landlord and author; the Black Power politics of 1970s Britain, which invade the house Moses wants to keep for himself; police racism; and, in Dawes's reading of the trilogy, identity and belonging, as Moses discovers how English his values have become. Writing is itself a subject: the memoirs pursue the ambition with which The Lonely Londoners ends.
summary: A comedy of Moses' rise from tenant to landlord and would-be memoirist, set in a house that fills with the politics and people of 1970s black London.
research_notes: Not read. The summary rests on the Penguin Modern Classics description, seen in several booksellers' copies as search-result extracts, and on an AbeBooks listing; the record is therefore partially verified. Bob's background, the narrative voice and the ending are not described in the sources consulted and are not stated.

title: Moses Migrating
description: The last of the Moses novels, published by Longman in Harlow in 1983, five years after Selvon moved to Canada. It won the Georges Bugnet Award for the novel at the Alberta Literary Awards in 1984.
plot_or_argument: More than twenty-five years after he became one of the 'Lonely Londoners', Moses Aloetta, though an avowed Anglophile, hankers for Trinidad, for sunshine, Carnival and rum punch, and the novel tells of his re-encounter with his native land (Lynne Rienner synopsis). In Dawes's account he at last musters the courage to return and must cope with recognising that he has become thoroughly and yet peculiarly English in his values, his sense of the world and his perception of himself.
narrative_structure: Framed by the return journey; the events in Trinidad are not described in the sources consulted.
meter_and_prosody: The publisher speaks of Selvon's characteristic irony and delicacy of touch; Dawes includes it in the comic trilogy.
historical_context: Published in 1983, after Selvon himself had left London for Calgary; the trilogy's homecoming came from a writer who had already left Britain for Canada.
literary_significance: Georges Bugnet Award (1984). Reissued by Lynne Rienner, Boulder, in 2009 with an introduction by Susheila Nasta.
bibliographical_notes: First edition: Longman, Harlow, 1983 (South Asian Britain; Toronto Metropolitan University Library). Reissued by Lynne Rienner, Boulder, 2009, with an introduction by Susheila Nasta.
thematic_analysis: Return migration, Anglophilia and the colonial's divided loyalties, and the migrant seeing his homeland as a stranger.
summary: Moses, more than twenty-five years after The Lonely Londoners, goes back from London to Trinidad.
research_notes: Not read. The account rests on the publisher's synopsis reprinted by Toronto Metropolitan University Library and on Dawes; the plot in Trinidad is not described in either.

title: Eldorado West One
description: Seven one-act plays, published by Peepal Tree Press in Leeds in 1988 and edited with an introduction and notes by Susheila Nasta. Selvon turned several of his novels and stories into scripts for the BBC, and these plays bring to dramatic life characters first seen in The Lonely Londoners and Moses Ascending.
plot_or_argument: The publisher's description asks whether Moses Aloetta, after long hard years in 'the Old Brit'n', will ever save enough money to go home to Trinidad, and answers that he will not if 'those damn vagabonds and reprobates', Sir Galahad, Cap and Harris, his so-called friends, have anything to do with it. The plays stage dreams and schemes, summer gaiety and winter disappointments, the experience of the parents and grandparents of today's Black British children, with Selvon's humour and poignancy.
narrative_structure: Seven separate one-act plays for radio; their titles and order were not checked.
literary_form: Plays (seven one-act radio plays, edited by Susheila Nasta)
meter_and_prosody: Louis James, reviewing the book in Wasafiri, called them vivid radio plays that teachers wishing to dramatise Selvon's colourful stories would welcome.
historical_context: Wikipedia dates Selvon's conversion of novels and stories into BBC radio scripts to the 1960s and 1970s; the collection appeared in 1988, ten years after he left Britain.
literary_significance: One of two books that preserve some of Selvon's work for radio, of which South Asian Britain counts more than twenty plays.
bibliographical_notes: Peepal Tree Press, Leeds, 1988 (South Asian Britain; Toronto Metropolitan University Library; Dawes; Wikipedia's text), ISBN 9780948833069, 156 pp. Wikipedia's list gives 1989; the publisher's page gives 6 January 1998, presumably a reprint.
thematic_analysis: Migrant life in London, the dream of return and the friendships and small exploitations among 'the boys'.
summary: Seven one-act radio plays about Moses Aloetta and his friends Sir Galahad, Cap and Harris in London.
research_notes: Not read. The account rests on the publisher's description; the titles and broadcast dates of the plays are not recorded.

title: Foreday Morning: Selected Prose 1946-1986
description: A selection of Selvon's prose from 1946 to 1986, edited by Kenneth Ramchand and Susheila Nasta and published by Longman in London in 1989. Wikipedia notes that much of the writing he did in Trinidad between 1945 and 1950 is found in it.
plot_or_argument: The book gathers prose from four decades of Selvon's career. Its earliest pieces belong to his years on the Trinidad Guardian, when he wrote stories and descriptive pieces under the names Michael Wentworth, Esses, Ack-Ack and Big Buffer; Dawes classes the book as nonfiction. The individual contents were not examined.
narrative_structure: A selection covering 1946-1986, made by two editors; its arrangement was not examined.
literary_form: Selected prose (edited by Kenneth Ramchand and Susheila Nasta)
meter_and_prosody: Not examined; the earliest pieces were journalism and short fiction written for a Trinidad newspaper.
historical_context: Published in 1989, a year after Susheila Nasta's Critical Perspectives on Sam Selvon (1988) and in the year Warwick gave Selvon an honorary doctorate.
literary_significance: The principal printed source for Selvon's early Trinidad writing, according to Wikipedia.
bibliographical_notes: Longman, London, 1989, edited by Kenneth Ramchand and Susheila Nasta (South Asian Britain; Wikipedia; Dawes).
thematic_analysis: As a retrospective selection it spans Selvon's subjects from Trinidad in the 1940s to life abroad; its themes are not analysed because the contents were not seen.
summary: Stories, sketches and other prose from forty years, beginning with Selvon's newspaper writing in Trinidad.
research_notes: Contents not examined; the individual pieces are not recorded.

title: Highway in the Sun and Other Plays
description: Four plays that Selvon wrote for BBC broadcast in the 1970s, published by Peepal Tree Press in Leeds in December 1991. The publisher presents them as his most focused treatment of the choice Indians in the Caribbean must make between tradition and creolisation; three adapt his Trinidad novels.
plot_or_argument: Highway in the Sun tells of Tiger and Urmilla's first year of marriage away from their extended family and of their dealings with Joe and Rita, their Afro-Creole neighbours, the matter of A Brighter Sun. In Home Sweet India Johnny, dismayed by his family's loss of culture, plans to return to India. In Turn Again Tiger, Tiger learns that he cannot turn his back on the Indian past if he is to lay its ghosts to rest and face the future whole. In Harvest in Wilderness the traditional cane-cutting world of Balgobin confronts the new technology of his creolised nephew Romesh, the conflict of The Plains of Caroni, 'but the past continues to spring surprises'.
narrative_structure: Four separate plays; three adapt the novels A Brighter Sun, Turn Again Tiger and The Plains of Caroni, while Home Sweet India has no novel behind it in the sources consulted.
literary_form: Plays (four plays first broadcast by the BBC)
meter_and_prosody: Written for broadcast by the BBC, according to the publisher; their language and dramatic form were not examined.
historical_context: The Anthurium special issue dates the BBC production of Home Sweet India to 1970, and Wikipedia and South Asian Britain list it among Selvon's television scripts; the book appeared in 1991, when he lived in Calgary.
literary_significance: It gathers Selvon's drama of Indo-Trinidadian life as Eldorado West One gathers his London plays; Dawes cites it as the compilation of his dramatic works.
bibliographical_notes: Peepal Tree Press, Leeds, 1 December 1991 (publisher), ISBN 9780948833076, 215 pp.; reprinted 2008 (Toronto Metropolitan University Library).
thematic_analysis: Tradition against creolisation among Indo-Trinidadians, return to India as a dream of recovered culture, marriage and friendship across ethnic lines, and the cane fields facing mechanisation.
summary: Highway in the Sun, Home Sweet India, Turn Again Tiger and Harvest in Wilderness.
research_notes: Not read. The account rests on the publisher's description. Which plays were made for radio and which for television is not stated; Wikipedia describes both books of plays as radio scripts but names Home Sweet India as a television script, hence the two genres.

title: Church Going
description: Church Going is a poem by Philip Larkin, written in 1954 and first published in his collection The Less Deceived (Marvell Press, 1955). An agnostic cyclist stops at an empty country church and, half mocking his own awkward reverence, asks what churches will become when belief has gone and why such buildings still draw him. It is generally regarded as one of his masterpieces.
plot_or_argument: Making sure nothing is going on inside, the speaker lets the door close behind him and takes off his cycle-clips in awkward reverence. He notes the flowers, the brass and the organ, runs a hand over the font, mounts the lectern and reads a few verses, ending 'Here endeth' much more loudly than he meant, signs the book and donates an Irish sixpence, deciding the place was not worth stopping for. Yet he did stop, as he often does, and he wonders what he is looking for. When churches fall out of use, will they be kept as museums, left to the rain and sheep, or visited by women with children for luck and cures? Who will be the last to seek the place for what it was: a scholar of rood-lofts, a lover of ruins, a Christmas-addict, or someone like himself, bored and uninformed but drawn to the spot where marriage, birth and death were solemnised? The final stanza answers with a tone of settled conviction: the building's air holds all our compulsions, recognised and robed as destinies, and someone will always discover in himself a hunger to be more serious and gravitate to this ground, which he once heard was proper to grow wise in, if only because so many dead lie round.
narrative_structure: Seven nine-line stanzas in iambic pentameter, rhymed, moving from anecdote to speculation and to a closing stanza of grave statement.
meter_and_prosody: Colloquial, self-deprecating narration ('brass and stuff / Up at the holy end') that rises into formal, almost liturgical cadence at the close; precise physical detail and comic deflation.
historical_context: Drafted from April 1954 through some twenty-one pages, abandoned and resumed, and finished in July 1954 while Larkin was sub-librarian at Queen's University, Belfast; The Less Deceived made his reputation the following year.
literary_significance: One of the best-known English poems of the century, and the poem that fixed the image of Larkin as the cycle-clipped, unillusioned observer; it is among his most anthologised and studied works.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Less Deceived (Hessle: The Marvell Press, November 1955, dated October). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F (p. 788).
thematic_analysis: The poem measures the decline of religious belief against the survival of the needs religion served. Its irony is directed at the speaker as much as at the church, and the joking inventory gives way to respect for a place where the great events of life were made serious. It is agnostic without being dismissive, and ends on the human need for seriousness and on the presence of the dead.
summary: The speaker's visit to an empty church: his inventory of its furnishings, the words he reads aloud from the lectern, the Irish sixpence he leaves; his speculation about what the building will become when no one uses it; and his conclusion that it remains 'a serious house on serious earth'.
critical_context: Wikipedia's article calls it generally regarded as one of his masterpieces, and notes Martin Amis's remark on the cycle-clips associated with Larkin in the popular imagination and Christopher Hitchens's on Larkin's fondness for church architecture beside his scepticism about Christianity.
research_notes: Whether the poem appeared in a periodical before The Less Deceived was not checked. The stanza count and metre are stated from the text, not from a consulted source.

title: MCMXIV
description: MCMXIV, the year 1914 in Roman numerals as on a war memorial, is a poem by Philip Larkin completed in May 1960 and first published in The Whitsun Weddings (Faber, 1964). A single sentence over four stanzas, without a main verb, it looks at what seems a photograph of volunteers queuing to enlist in August 1914 and at the England around them, and ends: 'Never such innocence again'.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens on the lines of men standing patiently as if outside a cricket or football ground, their moustached, archaic faces grinning as if the war were an August Bank Holiday lark. It widens to the streets behind them, with shops shut and blinds drawn, farthings and sovereigns, children at play called after kings and queens, tin advertisements for cocoa and twist and pubs open all day, and then to the countryside, where the place names are hidden under the summer grass and the servants live in tiny rooms in huge houses. The last stanza turns to judgement: never such innocence before or since, which became the past without a word, with the men leaving the gardens tidy and the thousands of marriages lasting a little while longer. The war that ended this world is never described; the poem knows, as its people cannot, what is about to happen to them.
narrative_structure: Four eight-line stanzas forming one sentence with no main verb, built of noun phrases, so that the scene stays suspended in time until the closing lines.
literary_form: Poem (four eight-line stanzas forming one sentence)
meter_and_prosody: Rhymed short lines, a catalogue of period detail and a restrained, elegiac cadence, with the Roman-numeral title recalling the inscriptions on war memorials.
historical_context: Completed on 17 May 1960; collected in The Whitsun Weddings, published by Faber on 28 February 1964, the book that established Larkin with a wider public.
literary_significance: One of the best-known English poems about the First World War written after it, often taught beside the poems of the war poets; its closing line has become proverbial.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Whitsun Weddings (London: Faber and Faber, 1964), according to Wikipedia. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F (p. 789).
thematic_analysis: The poem mourns the end of an England of settled hierarchy and unquestioning patriotism, and also the innocence of men who did not know what they were volunteering for. Its knowledge of the outcome, held back until the last stanza, turns a photograph into an elegy for a generation and a social order.
summary: The long queues of men outside the recruiting offices; the shut shops, the coins and advertisements, the children named after kings and queens; the countryside and the great houses with their servants; and the closing lament for an innocence that changed into the past without a word.
research_notes: Wikipedia's article on the poem is short and flagged as resting on one source. The details of the summary are stated from the text.

title: Talking in Bed
description: Talking in Bed is a short poem by Philip Larkin, completed in August 1960 and collected in The Whitsun Weddings (1964), about a couple for whom talk in bed, which ought to be easiest, has become difficult.
plot_or_argument: Talking in bed ought to be easiest, the speaker begins, since lying together is an emblem of two people being honest; yet more and more time passes in silence. Outside the wind builds and disperses clouds and dark towns heap up on the horizon, and none of it cares for the couple. Nothing explains why, at this unique distance from isolation, it becomes still harder to find words at once true and kind, or not untrue and not unkind.
narrative_structure: Twelve lines in four three-line stanzas, loosely rhymed, ending on a self-correcting double negative.
meter_and_prosody: Plain statement, a single image of wind and towns, and a final litotes ('not untrue and not unkind') that enacts the hesitation it describes.
historical_context: One of the poems of love and marriage in The Whitsun Weddings, written in the year of 'MCMXIV'.
literary_significance: Frequently anthologised and taught; its last lines are among Larkin's most quoted.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in The Whitsun Weddings (London: Faber and Faber, 1964). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F (p. 790).
thematic_analysis: Intimacy that does not abolish loneliness, and the conflict between honesty and kindness in what lovers say; the indifferent world outside sharpens the couple's isolation.
summary: A couple lying together in silence; the wind, clouds and dark towns outside; and the closing difficulty of finding words at once true and kind.
critical_context: A stylistic study in the University of Buckingham's Journal of Language and Literature reads the ending as a conflict between Grice's maxim of quality and the politeness principle.
research_notes: Earlier periodical publication, if any, was not checked.

title: High Windows (poem)
description: High Windows is the title poem of Philip Larkin's last collection, High Windows (Faber, 1974), completed in February 1967. An older man watching a young couple imagines their sexual freedom as the paradise his generation dreamed of, wonders whether his own freedom from religion once looked like paradise to his elders, and ends not in words but in an image of high windows and endless blue air.
plot_or_argument: Seeing a couple of kids, the speaker guesses that the boy is sleeping with the girl and that she takes the pill or wears a diaphragm, and he knows this is the paradise everyone old has dreamed of, with bonds and gestures pushed aside like an outdated combine harvester and the young sliding endlessly down to happiness. He wonders whether anyone looked at him forty years earlier and thought the same: no God any more, no sweating in the dark about hell, no hiding what you think of the priest, who will go down the long slide too, like free bloody birds. Then, rather than words, comes the thought of high windows: the sun-comprehending glass and, beyond it, the deep blue air that shows nothing, and is nowhere, and is endless.
narrative_structure: Five four-line stanzas, loosely rhymed, with a turn at the last stanza from argument to image.
meter_and_prosody: Obscenity and slang in the opening lines set against the lyrical abstraction of the close, a contrast characteristic of late Larkin.
historical_context: Completed on 12 February 1967, the year of the Sexual Offences Act and of rapidly changing sexual mores, while Larkin lived in the top flat of 32 Pearson Park, Hull, whose windows are widely believed to have suggested the image.
literary_significance: One of Larkin's most celebrated and discussed poems, and the title piece of the collection Clive James called 'despair made beautiful'.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in High Windows (London: Faber and Faber, 1974), the sixth of its twenty-four poems. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F (p. 790). The collection has its own record, High Windows.
thematic_analysis: Envy of the young and the recognition that each generation's liberation looks like paradise only from outside; the loss of religious fear and of religious hope together. The ending offers a vision that is either transcendence or blank emptiness, and refuses to choose.
summary: The speaker's coarse imagining of a young couple's sex life; the reflection that every generation envies the next its freedom, and that his own youth was free of God and hell; and the final image of sun-filled glass and empty sky.
research_notes: Wikipedia's article on the poem says the windows are mentioned 'after a funeral has been evoked'; no funeral is evoked in the text, and the statement is not used. The reference to the 1967 Act is context supplied here, not a claim of the sources about the poem.

title: Going, Going
description: Going, Going is a poem by Philip Larkin commissioned by the Department of the Environment and first printed in its working party report on the human habitat, How Do You Want to Live? (1972), then collected in High Windows (1974). It foresees the English countryside lost to development and profit.
plot_or_argument: The speaker had thought the sense of fields and farms beyond the town would last his time, and that the earth would always recover however it was abused. Now he doubts it, or perhaps is only getting old: the young crowd in the motorway cafe want more houses, more parking, more caravan sites, more pay, and the business pages approve takeovers that move industry into the unspoilt dales. Before he dies, he thinks, the whole country will be bricked in except for the tourist parts, the first slum of Europe; and that will be England gone, the shadows, meadows, lanes, guildhalls and carved choirs surviving only in books and galleries. Most things are never meant, he ends, but the greeds and garbage are too thick-strewn to be swept up now: he thinks it will happen soon.
narrative_structure: Nine six-line stanzas, rhymed, moving from memory through satire of the present to prophecy.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational, sardonic and plain, with lists of modern clutter set against a lyrical inventory of the England being lost.
historical_context: Completed on 25 January 1972 for the report of a Department of the Environment working party; Her Majesty's Stationery Office gave permission for its inclusion in High Windows.
literary_significance: Larkin's best-known public poem and an early literary statement of environmental anxiety in Britain, often quoted in debates about planning and the countryside.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in How Do You Want to Live? A Report on the Human Habitat (London: HMSO, 1972); collected in High Windows (Faber, 1974). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F (p. 791).
thematic_analysis: Environmental and cultural loss, the commercial greed behind it, and the speaker's suspicion that his alarm may be partly the pessimism of age.
summary: The speaker's former confidence that the fields would last his time; the demands for more houses, parking and caravan sites; the business pages and takeover bids; and the prophecy that England will be gone, leaving concrete and tyres.
research_notes: The report's title is given in the Hull archive catalogue as 'Human Habitat: how do you want to live'. Secondary commentary seen only in search results says the report printed the poem with passages cut; this was not confirmed and is not stated in the record.

title: Sad Steps
description: Sad Steps is a poem by Philip Larkin, completed in April 1968 and collected in High Windows (1974). Its title comes from Sir Philip Sidney's sonnet 'With how sad steps, O Moon, thou climb'st the skies'; Larkin's sad steps are a middle-aged man's on his way back to bed.
plot_or_argument: Groping back to bed after a piss, the speaker parts the curtains and is startled by the rapid clouds and the moon's cleanliness over the wedge-shadowed gardens. There is something laughable about the moon dashing through cloud, high and preposterous and separate, and he tries out and rejects the romantic apostrophes ('Lozenge of love! Medallion of art!'). Instead he shivers: the hardness, brightness and far-reaching singleness of its stare remind him of the strength and pain of being young, which cannot come again but is for others undiminished somewhere.
narrative_structure: Eighteen lines in six three-line stanzas, rhymed, turning on the word 'No' from mockery to reflection.
meter_and_prosody: A crude opening, a parody of high poetic diction in the middle, and a sober, generous close.
historical_context: Completed on 24 April 1968, during the years of the poems of ageing and mortality that make up much of High Windows.
literary_significance: A much-anthologised example of Larkin's dialogue with the English lyric tradition, here with Sidney's Astrophil and Stella.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in High Windows (London: Faber and Faber, 1974), seventeenth of its poems. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F (p. 793).
thematic_analysis: Ageing and the loss of youth; the gap between poetic convention and plain experience, closed at the end by a plainness that honours the moon instead of decorating it.
summary: The speaker's sight of the moon at four in the morning; his mockery of the poetic moon; and his sober recognition of what it reminds him of.
research_notes: The summary is stated from the text; an essay in 3 Quarks Daily (2016) was seen only as a search extract. The source of the title in Astrophil and Stella, sonnet 31, is stated from general knowledge.

title: Homage to a Government
description: Homage to a Government is an ironic poem by Philip Larkin about the British withdrawal of its forces from east of Suez because the country could no longer pay for them. Completed in January 1969, it first appeared in The Sunday Times and was collected in High Windows (1974).
plot_or_argument: Next year, the poem begins, we are to bring the soldiers home for lack of money, and it is all right: the places they guarded must guard themselves, and we want the money for ourselves at home instead of working. It is hard to say who wanted it, but nobody minds; the places are far off, and from what we hear the soldiers only made trouble. Next year we shall live in a country that brought its soldiers home for lack of money; the statues will stand in the same tree-muffled squares, our children will not know it is a different country, and all we can hope to leave them now is money.
narrative_structure: Three six-line stanzas whose line endings repeat key words (home, right, orderly, money), giving the poem the sound of a flat, repeated excuse.
meter_and_prosody: Deadpan irony, the government's own reassuring idiom turned against it.
historical_context: Written after the Labour government's decision, announced in January 1968, to withdraw British forces from east of Suez by 1971; a commentator quotes Larkin calling the withdrawal for reasons of cost 'a dreadful humiliation'.
literary_significance: Larkin's most explicitly political poem, often cited in discussions of his conservatism and of the literature of Britain's imperial decline.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Sunday Times, 19 January 1969 (according to a South24 article); collected in High Windows (Faber, 1974). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F (p. 793).
thematic_analysis: The end of empire seen as national humiliation and moral decline, with complacency and the love of money replacing duty.
summary: The announcement that the soldiers are to come home for lack of money; the repeated assurance that this is all right; and the picture of a country whose statues stand unchanged while it has become a different country.
research_notes: The Sunday Times date and Larkin's remark rest on one source (South24, which reads the poem as being about Aden); Gale's Poetry for Students, seen as a search extract, describes it as criticising the withdrawal of the last British troops from bases east of Suez. The 1968 announcement is stated from general historical knowledge.

title: The Explosion
description: The Explosion is a poem by Philip Larkin, completed in January 1970 and placed last in his final collection, High Windows (1974). It describes the morning of a mining disaster, the men walking to the pit, the tremor at noon, and the moment in which their widows, hearing the promises of the funeral service, see the dead transfigured.
plot_or_argument: On the day of the explosion, shadows point towards the pithead and the slagheap sleeps in the sun. Men in pitboots come down the lane, coughing oath-edged talk and pipe-smoke; one chases rabbits, loses them, and comes back with a nest of lark's eggs, which he shows the others and puts back in the grass. Fathers, brothers, nicknames, laughter, they pass through the tall gates. At noon there is a tremor; cows stop chewing for a second, and the sun dims as in a heat-haze. The explosion itself and the deaths underground are never shown. In italic lines the language of the chapel promises that the dead go on before us and that we shall see them face to face; and for a second the wives see the men of the explosion larger than in life, gold as on a coin, walking somehow from the sun towards them, one showing the eggs unbroken.
narrative_structure: Twenty-five lines: eight unrhymed three-line stanzas and a final isolated line, in trochaic tetrameter with variations, the measure of Longfellow's Hiawatha.
literary_form: Poem (eight unrhymed tercets and a single line)
meter_and_prosody: Spare, concrete narration in clipped clauses, a shift to a formal, scriptural register in the italic stanza, and a visionary close unusual in Larkin.
historical_context: Completed on 5 January 1970. Larkin's papers include correspondence with the Poem of the Month Club about reprinting it in High Windows, of which it is the last poem.
literary_significance: One of Larkin's most admired late poems, often read as a counterweight to his scepticism because it grants the religious vision a moment of reality; widely anthologised and taught.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in High Windows (London: Faber and Faber, 1974), the last of its twenty-four poems. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F (p. 794).
thematic_analysis: Sudden death in an ordinary working day, the solidarity of a mining community, and the consolations of religious language, which the poem allows a moment of truth without asserting it. The unbroken eggs become a symbol of the wholeness of the men's lives, or of life continuing.
summary: Miners walking to the pithead on a sunny morning; one of them finding a nest of lark's eggs and putting it back; the tremor at noon; words of consolation from the chapel; and the wives' vision of their men walking towards them, one showing the eggs unbroken.
research_notes: The correspondence with the Poem of the Month Club implies an earlier printing by the club, whose date was not established, so 1974 is recorded as the first publication in a book. Accounts that Larkin was prompted by a television documentary on mining in late 1969 were seen only on study sites and are not used. The EBSCO entry was seen as a search extract.

title: This Be The Verse
description: This Be The Verse is a poem by Philip Larkin, first published in the August 1971 issue of New Humanist and collected in High Windows (1974). Its profane first line about parents and its advice not to have children have made it one of the most quoted English poems of the century.
plot_or_argument: Your parents mess you up, the speaker says in far blunter words: they do not mean to, but they fill you with their faults and add some extra just for you. They were messed up in their turn by fools in old-style hats and coats, who were half the time soppy-stern and half at one another's throats. Man hands on misery to man; it deepens like a coastal shelf. Get out as early as you can, the poem ends, and don't have any kids yourself: the only way to stop the inheritance is to refuse to pass it on.
narrative_structure: Three four-line stanzas of rhymed iambic tetrameter, the neat form of a hymn or epitaph.
meter_and_prosody: Shocking colloquial obscenity in a strict, light-verse form; the title parodies Robert Louis Stevenson's 'Requiem' ('This be the verse you grave for me').
historical_context: Completed in April 1971 and first printed in New Humanist, the journal of the Rationalist Press Association, in August 1971.
literary_significance: Larkin's most quoted poem, endlessly cited and parodied; Wikipedia, citing the Oxford Companion to Modern Poetry, notes its dark humour, directness and taboo-breaking language.
bibliographical_notes: First published in New Humanist, August 1971; collected in High Windows (Faber, 1974). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F (p. 795). Also spelled This Be the Verse.
thematic_analysis: Inherited unhappiness and the impossibility of good parenting, presented as a universal law with a comic bleakness that critics read both as despair and as ironic tenderness.
summary: The claim that parents pass on their faults to their children; the observation that their own parents did the same; and the conclusion that misery is handed down and the only escape is to have no children.
research_notes: Wikipedia's article carries a citation flagged as not a real article; only its publication facts, which agree with the collection's table of completion dates, are used. The summary paraphrases the text.

title: Politics and the English Language
description: Politics and the English Language is an essay by George Orwell, first published in the April 1946 issue of the monthly Horizon and collected in Shooting an Elephant and Other Essays (1950). It argues that the English of its time was ugly and inaccurate, that slovenly language and foolish thought reinforce each other, and that political language in particular is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable. It closes with six rules for clear writing, and has become one of the most reprinted essays in English.
plot_or_argument: Orwell begins by rejecting the view that the decline of English is a natural, irreversible process. Language becomes ugly and inaccurate because our thoughts are foolish, but its slovenliness makes it easier to have foolish thoughts, as a man may drink because he feels a failure and then fail the more completely because he drinks; the process can be reversed by people willing to take the trouble. He quotes five passages, by Harold Laski, Lancelot Hogben, an essay on psychology in the American magazine Politics, a communist pamphlet and a letter to Tribune, and draws from them a catalogue of swindles and perversions: dying metaphors used without thought of their meaning, 'operators or verbal false limbs' that pad sentences with phrases instead of verbs, pretentious diction that dresses up bias as impartial and scientific, and meaningless words, common in art and literary criticism and in political terms such as democracy and fascism. Modern prose, he says, consists less of words chosen for their meaning than of phrases tacked together like the sections of a prefabricated henhouse, and he demonstrates it by translating a verse of Ecclesiastes ('the race is not to the swift') into modern English of the worst sort. Political speech and writing are largely the defence of the indefensible: the bombing of defenceless villages is called pacification, the expulsion of peasants transfer of population, imprisonment without trial elimination of unreliable elements. Orthodoxy demands a lifeless, imitative style, and the great enemy of clear language is insincerity: when there is a gap between real and declared aims, one turns to long words and exhausted idioms like a cuttlefish spurting out ink. Ready-made phrases think for the writer and can even conceal his meaning from himself. Orwell proposes that a writer should let the meaning choose the words, and offers six rules: never use a figure of speech you are used to seeing in print; never use a long word where a short one will do; cut every word you can; never use the passive where you can use the active; never use a foreign phrase, scientific word or jargon if there is an everyday English equivalent; and break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous. He concedes that his own essay commits the faults it attacks, insists that he is concerned with language as an instrument for expressing thought, not with its literary use, and ends that political language is designed to give an appearance of solidity to pure wind, and that one can at least send some worn-out phrase into the dustbin where it belongs.
narrative_structure: An argumentative essay that moves from a general claim, through quoted specimens and a classified catalogue of faults, to the political analysis and the practical rules, ending with qualifications and a short peroration.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, concrete and vigorous prose, rich in homely analogies (the drinker, the cuttlefish, the prefabricated henhouse, the packet of aspirins at one's elbow), quoting its examples and parodying them; Orwell admits that the essay itself breaks some of its rules.
historical_context: Written in late 1945, when Orwell's payment book records it on 11 December, after the success of Animal Farm and the death of his wife; it was meant for George Weidenfeld's Contact, which turned it down, and appeared in Horizon almost at the same time as 'The Prevention of Literature', which shares its concern with truth and language under political pressure.
literary_significance: One of the most influential essays in English on style and on political language. Lynn Z. Bloom found it reprinted 118 times in 325 editions of 58 composition readers published between 1946 and 1996, and it remains a staple of writing courses; its phrases about making lies sound truthful and murder respectable are constantly quoted in discussion of political rhetoric.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Horizon, vol. 13, no. 76 (April 1946), pp. 252-265; collected in Shooting an Elephant and Other Essays (London: Secker and Warburg, 1950), which has its own record. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F (p. 596).
thematic_analysis: The essay ties the quality of prose to the quality of thought and of politics. Its central claim is that abstraction and euphemism allow writers and readers to accept atrocities they would reject if they were named concretely, so that clear language is a political and moral discipline. It treats stale language as a habit that thinks for the writer, and orthodoxy of any party as the enemy of individual, honest expression. The concern with how language can make certain thoughts impossible returns in the Newspeak of Nineteen Eighty-Four.
summary: Five specimen passages of bad contemporary prose; a catalogue of faults (dying metaphors, verbal false limbs, pretentious diction, meaningless words); a parody of a verse of Ecclesiastes in modern officialese; the analysis of political euphemism; the argument that insincerity is the great enemy of clear language; and six rules, with the claim that the decline of the language is reversible.
critical_context: Michael Shelden called it Orwell's most important essay on style, while Bernard Crick's biography did not mention it. John Rodden notes Orwell's own admission that he commits the faults he attacks; Terry Eagleton praised its demystification of political language before turning against Orwell; Carl Freedman's 1981 article on the essay and English composition started a debate about its ideology. The linguist Geoffrey Pullum has called it dishonest and its insistence on avoiding familiar phrases unfollowable, and Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage notes that Orwell uses the passive in a little over 20 per cent of its sentences, more than the periodicals surveyed.
research_notes: Publication details, the payment-book date and the history with Contact are from Wikipedia's article, which cites the Orwell bibliography, D. J. Taylor (2003) and the New Oxford Review; the article carries a 'more citations needed' banner. The link to Newspeak is a common critical observation, stated here without a specific source.

title: Waiting for Aunty to Cough
description: Waiting for Aunty to Cough is a comic story by Samuel Selvon about Brackley, a young West Indian in London, and his English girlfriend Beatrice. It appeared in the Evening Standard on 1 April 1957 and was collected the same year in the London part of Ways of Sunlight.
plot_or_argument: Brackley, who has taken up with a girl living far from central London, must see Beatrice home every night and make his way back late, missing buses and trains. One night she has forgotten her door key, and rather than rouse the household they wait in the cold outside the house in the early hours, hoping to hear Aunty cough. Beatrice dozes on his arm while Brackley, folded into the small doorway, cramped and frozen, waits through the night. Between five and half past he thinks he hears Aunty cough and, to Beatrice's amazement and horror, pelts the house with a stone. Word gets round, and the boys never let him forget it, hailing him with 'Brackley! You still waiting for Aunty to cough?'
narrative_structure: An anecdote framed as a story told among 'the boys', ending on their catch-phrase.
meter_and_prosody: Selvon's creolised narrative voice, with Trinidadian syntax and idiom carrying the comedy.
historical_context: One of the London stories of Ways of Sunlight (1957), written in the years of The Lonely Londoners and of the Windrush migration; Selvon's papers at the University of the West Indies hold its manuscript and the Evening Standard clipping.
literary_significance: A frequently anthologised example of Selvon's comic London writing and of his use of Caribbean speech in narration.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the Evening Standard (London), 1 April 1957, under a 'London Calypso' heading, according to the finding aid of the Sam Selvon Collection; collected in Ways of Sunlight (London: MacGibbon and Kee, 1957), which has its own record. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F (p. 737).
thematic_analysis: The comedy of a West Indian immigrant negotiating English suburban propriety and an interracial romance, told as a 'lime', the Trinidadian gathering where such stories are shared.
summary: Brackley's nightly journeys to see Beatrice home to the far suburbs; a night when she has forgotten her key and they wait outside for her aunt to cough; his violent solution at dawn; and the joke the boys make of it.
research_notes: The plot rests on an essay on Selvon's stories in Thresholds (University of Chichester) and on the text; the Evening Standard date comes from the collection's finding aid, seen as search extracts because the archive server was unavailable. The Thresholds author's recollection of hearing Selvon read it on Caribbean Voices was not confirmed.
